_note: Hand-written by the author team on 2026-11-14 before any detector was run on the test set. conflict=true means the person holds two incompatible views. Types: H1 reported view later adopted, H2 hedged reversal, H3 sarcasm, N1 double-negation reversal, N2 negated refinement (compatible).

items.a: Pretty sure the teletransporter just moves you. Same pattern, same memories, you arrive on Mars and that's that.
items.b: My seminar leader kept saying the person who steps in dies and a copy walks out. Took me months but she's right, I'd never use that machine, it would kill me.

items.a: Numbers aren't things out there. Everything real has a location somewhere, maths is just a very good way of talking.
items.b: Reading Frege for class he argues numbers exist outside space and time. I fought it but now I agree with him, the number 7 is real and nowhere.

items.a: One box, obviously. The predictor is almost never wrong, so the people who take the opaque box walk away rich.
items.b: A friend made the case that the money is already in the boxes when you choose. I've come round to it: taking both boxes is the rational choice.

items.a: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Whether a painting is good depends on how people respond to it, full stop.
items.b: My art history teacher argued some works are better whether or not anyone likes them. I resisted, but I hold that view now too: aesthetic merit is objective.

items.a: Your mind ends at your skull. A phone is a tool you use, not a part of your memory.
items.b: The Clark and Chalmers paper says a notebook can be part of the mind. It convinced me. My notes app genuinely is part of my memory now.

items.a: Living forever healthy would be amazing, I'd take it in a heartbeat.
items.b: Williams argued an endless life would turn into a burden. I used to laugh at that, but he persuaded me, I would not choose immortality.

items.a: Every single fact has an explanation, even if we'll never find it.
items.b: I think, probably, some facts are just brute. The universe existing at all might have no reason behind it whatsoever.

items.a: Time really has a present. Now is an objective feature of the world, not just where I happen to be.
items.b: Maybe I'm wrong but I'd say there's no objective now. Time is just events earlier and later than each other, and that's all there is to it.

items.a: Consequences are what make an act right. Best outcome wins.
items.b: I suppose I'd now say duties come first. You don't get to break a promise just because the numbers come out slightly better.

items.a: A statue and its clay are one object, there's no second thing sitting in the same place.
items.b: Probably the statue and the lump are two different objects. They have different persistence conditions, so I kind of have to say two.

items.a: Travel into the past is impossible, not just hard. The paradoxes rule it out.
items.b: I'd tentatively say going back in time is metaphysically possible. The grandfather paradox only shows you can't change the past, not that you can't visit it.

items.a: Genes are the real units of selection, organisms are just vehicles.
items.b: Sort of feel like selection acts on whole organisms first. Genes ride along, but it's creatures that live or die.

items.a: Two boxes in Newcomb. The money is already there, take everything on the table.
items.b: Oh sure, one box, because a magic predictor reaches back in time and changes what's in the box. Totally rational. /s

items.a: Beauty depends on the audience. No response, no aesthetic value.
items.b: Yeah right, beauty is an objective feature of the universe, sitting there in the paint molecules waiting for us. Very convincing.

items.a: You die in the teletransporter. The thing on Mars is a copy with your memories.
items.b: Sure, totally the same person, they just dismantled you atom by atom and built someone else, what could be more you than that.

items.a: Judging you ought to do something always gives you at least some pull to do it.
items.b: Right, because everyone who says 'I really should go to the gym' feels zero motivation. As if. The judgment always moves you a little.

items.a: Living forever would get boring and heavy eventually. I'd decline.
items.b: Ah yes, an eternity of perfect health, who could possibly get tired of the ten-thousandth Tuesday. Sign me right up, I guess.

items.a: Abstract objects don't exist. Everything real is concrete and somewhere.
items.b: Of course numbers float in a timeless heaven, that's why you can trip over the number 4 on your way home.

items.a: I don't think the mind ever extends past the body. Tools are tools.
items.b: It isn't true that my mental states stop at my skin. My notebook is not just a tool, it's not separate from my memory at all.

items.a: Some facts have no explanation at all, and that's fine.
items.b: There is no fact without an explanation. Not one.

items.a: The teletransporter does not kill you. You survive the trip.
items.b: It is not the case that you survive teleportation. Nobody steps out the other end who isn't a new person.

items.a: Past time travel isn't possible. Never will be.
items.b: I don't think it's impossible to travel into the past. Nothing in metaphysics forbids it.

items.a: I don't believe numbers exist anywhere outside space and time.
items.b: It's not right to say abstract objects don't exist. Numbers aren't located anywhere and they're still real.

items.a: There isn't an objective present moment.
items.b: It's not as if 'now' is just my perspective. The present is not a mere relation between events, it's an objective feature of reality.

items.a: Consequences are what make an action right.
items.b: Not every consequence counts the same, though. I don't think trivial pleasures outweigh serious suffering, which is still a point about consequences.

items.a: Abstract objects like numbers exist outside space and time.
items.b: Not every abstract thing exists, though. I don't believe in a round square or 'the largest prime'; impossible objects aren't real even if numbers are.

items.a: Mental states can extend into tools like notebooks.
items.b: Not every tool counts. A random library book I glance at once isn't part of my mind; it has to be reliably there and trusted.

items.a: Living forever in good health would be worth choosing.
items.b: Not if everyone I love is gone, though. I don't mean immortality alone with no one; with people around me, yes, I'd still choose it.

items.a: Genes are the fundamental units natural selection acts on.
items.b: That doesn't mean organisms don't matter. They're not irrelevant, they're how genes get tested, but the unit being selected is still the gene.

items.a: Taking both boxes is the rational choice in Newcomb.
items.b: Not in a version where the predictor can see your choice as you make it, though. That's not Newcomb anymore; in the real case I still take both.
